title: Inquest begins under tight security:
article: A coroner's inquest into the death of 18-year-old Keyvan Tabesh, shot in 2003 by a Port Moody police officer, opened in a New Westminster courtroom with a high level of security Monday.
The officer who shot the Burnaby teen cannot be named because both he and his family have been receiving death threats directly related to the incident.

"There are some safety concerns with respect to the officer and we have taken steps to protect his safety," said Port Moody Police Department spokesperson Const. Phil Reid. He would not go into specifics about how the officer is being protected.

The inquest is being held in a high-security courtroom adjacent to the one where lawyers are making pretrial arguments in the Robert Pickton murder case. Coroner Liana Wright ruled in favour of a publication ban on the officer's name and image, an uncommon move.

"This security ... is among the highest security I've seen," said the officer's lawyer, Jack Harris. "We're doing the right thing for the physical security of a number of people. That's simply so he won't have to live under more threats than he already has to live under."

Shortly before 2 a.m. on July 14, 2003, two women reported that they had been attacked by a man with a machete while they were in their car outside of Sidepocket Billiards, near the intersection of Moray and St. John's streets.

They told police their vehicle had been bumped by a black Honda Prelude and an armed man had climbed out, threatened them, smashed the rear driver's side window of the car and hit the car with the machete.
While an officer was interviewing the two women, the Prelude drove by. The officer tried to follow the car and block it in on a nearby street, but it drove away.

Meanwhile, the officer involved in the shooting had been called in to investigate a robbery nearby, and was in plainclothes and driving an unmarked vehicle when he saw Tabesh's car pull into a cul- de-sac in the 2000 block of St. George Street.
Tabesh, wielding the machete, and a friend got out of the car and moved towards the police officer, who fired several shots at the pair, killing Tabesh and injuring his friend.
A firearms investigation done by members of the Vancouver Police Department determined that Tabesh was no further than 1.3 metres from the driver's side of the police officer's car when he was shot.
Tabesh's family just wants to know what actually happened that summer night.
Forough Jabalameli told reporters she wants the truth and doesn't want to see another incident like the one that took her son's life.

"I suffer a lot as a mother," she said. "Still I cannot believe it happened to my son. My son wasn't a kind of aggressive person the media try to introduce him as. He was a gentle, a kind person and I don't believe it happened to us. We came here for a better life and a better education. We didn't come here to be executed on the street by police."
The Tabesh family's lawyer, Don Morrison, said there is one goal to the inquest.

"At an inquest, the goal is to ensure that as best as possible that these type of things don't happen again. What happened to Keyvan shouldn't have happened. It just shouldn't have happened," he said.

Morrison said he would also like to see investigations into police shootings done differently. He said he will have an expert witness testify about a model used in Ontario where a special investigative unit, which is arm's length from police, investigates all police shootings.
He added that in Newfoundland, the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary has been known to invite another province into the investigation.
"You need that distance, that objectivity, so that you're not investigating a colleague and the investigation is truly going to have an objective analysis of what took place," Morrison said.
John Bethell, counsel for the coroner, said that's why there are inquests.

"There have been some suggestions in some corners that having the police investigate the police just discourages the public confidence. But that's one of the reasons we have an inquest, that's one of the reasons we have a police complaints commission and that's one of the reasons that we have any number of other agencies to make sure that the oversight is proper," he said.

After an internal investigation by the Port Moody Police Department, which was looked over by officers from the Vancouver Police Department, Crown counsel decided not to pursue charges against the 25-year veteran officer, who will give evidence Wednesday.
"I made sure this investigation was done fairly, honestly and I left no stone unturned ... I did it to the best of my ability," said Port Moody Sgt. Dave Wynes while giving evidence at the inquiry.
The inquiry continues.
